asDecan.p: Each sign is split into three slices of ten degrees, called decans, and each slice has its own ruling planet and its own small card. Your Sun falls between 10 and 19 degrees of Capricorn, the middle slice, where the sign has stopped arriving and is working at full strength. In the old Chaldean order Mars rules those ten degrees. That matters a lot, because Mars is exalted in Capricorn, which is the traditional way of saying the planet is treated as an honoured guest there and shows its most idealised side. Saturn still runs the sign, so underneath it's cardinal earth, ambitious and patient. What Mars adds is the appetite for actual effort, the hands-on part. The slice before yours is the Two of Pentacles, Jupiter's decan, and it's busy juggling. The one after is the Four, the Sun's, and it holds on to what it has. Yours is the bit in between, the man up on the bench in the picture with a chisel in his hand, still working.

You like work you can point at. The spreadsheet that finally balances, the shelf you put up that's still level three years later, the report nobody has to send back. In a meeting you're the one who asks who's actually doing each part and by when, and people find that either a relief or slightly annoying. At a family dinner you end up fixing the tap nobody mentioned. A Sunday with nothing planned usually lasts until about eleven before you've found a job, and you'd call that relaxing. You're competitive in a quiet way. You don't need to win out loud, you just need to know your part was done properly, and ideally better than the last person managed. When a friend asks for help moving house you turn up with your own tape and a system for labelling the boxes.

The less obvious gift is how well you take criticism of the work. Mars is exalted here, so the fight in you tends to go into the job itself, and when someone tells you the plan has a flaw your first reaction is usually interest. A manager marks up your draft in red and you're a bit pleased, because now it'll be better. You give feedback the same way, straight and about the thing, and people who've worked with you tend to trust it because it's never really about them. That makes you unusually good in a team of specialists, the builder who'll listen to the architect and the architect who'll listen to the builder. It also makes you a good teacher, if a slightly exacting one. Younger colleagues often remember you years later as the person who showed them how to do it properly and didn't make them feel stupid.

The shadow is quieter than overwork. You tend to rate people by the quality of what they produce, and you're often unaware you're doing it. A colleague who's lovely but sloppy gets filed under unreliable and never quite gets out of that file. Your brother-in-law assembles the flat-pack wardrobe and you say nothing, and then, once everyone's gone to bed, you take the doors off and rehang them. That's Mars, which wants to act, meeting Saturn's sign, which wants it done to standard. The people around you notice the rehung doors. What they hear is that their help wasn't good enough, and after a few of those they stop offering. There's an inward version as well. You can have a perfectly decent year and only really remember the two jobs you'd have done differently.

When something goes wrong your first move is to work. A redundancy, a breakup, a parent going into care, and within a day you've made a list, rung the people who need ringing and started on whatever can be fixed. That's genuinely useful, and in a crisis you're the one others lean on. The trouble comes about a week later, when the practical jobs run out and the feeling is still sitting there. So you find new jobs. You clean out the garage, take on a second project, stay back at the office. The people close to you can end up feeling shut out, because you're busy in the next room when they wanted to sit with you. What helps is something physical with no outcome, a long swim, a hard walk up a hill, digging a bed you don't need. After that, tell one person what actually happened and how it felt.

You love by doing, and anyone who's been out with you for long has noticed it. The car gets serviced, the leaking gutter gets done, their CV gets rewritten at eleven at night. What's less obvious is that you fall for competence. Someone who's very good at their job, or cooks properly, or can get an old engine going, gets your attention faster than someone who's merely charming. The best relationships for this decan usually have a shared project in them early, a house, a business, a garden, a long trip that takes planning, because working side by side is how you get close. The risk is the relationship itself becoming the project, with stages and a schedule, and a partner who starts to feel a bit managed. Physically Mars here is patient and steady, and you show desire in a plain, unfussy way that most people find reassuring.

The Devil is your Sun card, and it gives you the ambition and a clear eye for how power works in a place. This slice adds the craft underneath. You want to be very good at an actual thing, surgery or joinery or tax law or cutting hair, and you want the respect of people who can tell the difference. Trades, engineering, anything with an apprenticeship or a long training suits you, and so does any team where each person has a specialty and the job fails if one of them slacks. You tend to rise by being the one who knows how it's done. The usual mistake is staying on the tools too long. There comes a point where the business or the department needs you to plan and delegate, and you'd honestly prefer to be up the ladder doing it yourself. Take the promotion anyway, and keep one piece of hands-on work that stays yours.

At twenty this decan often seems older than it is. You're the one who had the part-time job all through uni, the savings account, the firm opinions about how the café should be run. You can be hard on people your own age who look like they're drifting. By the mid-thirties the pattern usually pays off in a visible way, a qualification finished, a small business with staff, a name in a narrow field, and that's when a lot of people with the Sun here notice they've built a great deal and rested very little. It's common to see a deliberate change around then, a new sport, a hobby with no income attached, a partner who insists on proper holidays. The fifties tend to be kind to this slice of Capricorn. The skill is deep by then, and there's often real pleasure in training someone younger and handing over part of what you made.

Once a month, pick one thing someone else has done for you and let it stand exactly as they did it. The dishwasher loaded their way, the email a colleague drafted, the seedlings your partner planted too close together. Don't fix it, don't mention it, and don't quietly redo it later when they've gone out. If the itch gets strong, go and do some hard physical work on something that's only yours, sand back a chair, knead bread for ten minutes. Then thank them for it.
